items.title: Thanksgiving Logistics
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Here's a friendly reminder that if you have a frozen turkey over 12 pounds, you should put it in the refrigerator to begin thawing today. If it's 12 pounds or smaller, you might be able to wait until Sunday or Monday. I got my 18-pounder out yesterday, because I've done this quite a few times.

If you are new to cooking Thanksgiving, this might be a good time to jot down your to-do list for the next week. Anything that can be prepared ahead of time, while keeping in mind how fresh it must be, should be listed on the appropriate day. For example, make cornbread on Tuesday, make the cornbread into dressing on Wednesday night, pop it in the oven Thursday. Remember, you will not have a lot of oven room with a turkey in there Thursday, so make sure your pies are done before cooking the bird. You may as well shop for everything you need now, except for fresh produce.

The one thing I forget every year is to take the second oven rack out of the oven before heating. I always have to remove a hot rack and set it out on the deck so no one gets burned. But that doesn't ruin any food, so I feel good that it's my one constant failure.

Oh, there will be other failures. Any big production, like a wedding, will have

go wrong. It's best just to laugh it off, because without a glitch or two, it would be hard to recall these occasions in future years.

items.title: Love on a Plate
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
This lovely animated vignette is about a family who spreads love to each, each in their own way. When the granddaughter veers from the traditional ways, she doesn't lose the love she was taught. She just has to find a way to put her own spin on her family's traditions. This story relies on the model of a zoetrope to convey its ideas, because the story is about the cyclical nature of life and how this family came full circle. Yes, they made real zoetrope discs to start the project. The result is both sweet and thought-provoking. You might want to send this to your grandmother.   

Directed by Ana G. Lacaze and produced by Jessica Heidt, Love on a Plate is part of a collection called

Pixar Artist's Short Films. If you are interested, there's also a behind the scenes video on how this animation was made, and what the Pixar Artist's Lab is all about.

items.title: The Day the President Moved Thanksgiving
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
This is more of a true story than it appears. Franklin Roosevelt changed Thanksgiving from the last Thursday in November to the next-to-the-last Thursday, in  order

to give retailers a longer Christmas shopping season. It was only in December of 1941 that congress set the date of Thanksgiving to the fourth Thursday in November, which can occur as early as the 22nd or as late as November 28th.

items.title: A Unique Piece of Amber
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Amber is hardened and fossilized tree resin. When resin (which is different from sap) falls on an animal, usually an insect, that body is preserved as is. That allows us to see prehistoric bugs as they appeared in life, with its original form preserved even if it is dessicated, encased in nature's glass.

This cricket encased in amber is a rare specimen, because it has a tiny gas bubble still in its abdomen. The bubble was most likely formed by chemical and bacterial action on whatever the cricket last ate, and it might be methane. In other words, it's a fart. It couldn't be expelled because resin is pretty thick before it turns to stone, and the cricket was dead anyway. But this bubble still moves when you turn the amber! That requires liquid, and with a little digging I found out that amber can contain water despite the resin's dehydrating properties under certain conditions. Cool. (via

Geeks Are Sexy)

items.title: Trying to Avoid a Cold
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: Cold and flu season are ramping up, so let's take two minutes to consider something you've never really thought about before. Where is the place you are most likely to run into someone who has a communicable illness? In bed, sure, but you can avoid other people's beds. You might say the doctor's office, but if you're willing to spend your time and money there, that means you're already pretty sick (at least in America). No, it's the store aisle where the cold remedies are. When there's a bug going around, that aisle is liable to be crowded with suspicious shoppers. You could order symptom relief through Door Dash, but those gig workers are desperate enough to work while sick, and will sneeze on your package.

items.title: Rich People Collecting Unicorn Horns
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Once you have enough money to buy all the fine objects and comforts available to you, the rich are left with a desire to be admired by others. The easy way to do that is to buy more stuff, as long as those objects are rare, expensive, and liable to draw attention. In the 16th and 17th centuries, there was a world of these curious objects available from world explorers and traders. Wealthy people collected exotic art from faraway places and natural specimens never seen before, or even better both in one object, into curiosity cabinets. Explaining these impressive objects raised one's status in a way mere money didn't, even when that explanation was nonsense. Evan Puschak explores the rise of curiosity cabinets and the forces that made them a thing. (via

kottke)

items.title: Authoritarian Fiction is Scarier Than Post-Apocalypse Dystopias
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Grim stories about the future come in two basic models. Some are about apocalyptic disasters, like a zombie uprising, an alien invasion, or a nuclear war that wipes out most of mankind, leaving our protagonists to figure out how to survive and start all over. That would include things like

Mad Max, A Boy and His Dog, The Book of Eli, and . 

Then there's the authoritarian dystopia, in which the population is still here, but kept under the thumb of an authoritarian government. The classic example is 1984, but it would also include

Soylent Green, The Handmaid's Tale, The Hunger Games, and . These stories are actually scarier, because they could more plausibly come true. In fact, most are based at least partly on events that have already happened somewhere at some time. To sum it up, apocalyptic disasters rely heavily on fantasy, while authoritarian fiction is a warning of what could happen if we aren't diligent. PBS picks these stories apart, and shows us how we might still slide down those paths.

items.title: How to Fix Our Attention Spans
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Much has been written about our shrinking attention spans in the last couple of decades, which coincidentally exploded with the introduction of smart phones and social media. Those accounts are mostly complaints instead of serious discussions of causes and remedies. You mostly notice shortened attention spans in other people, but if you are honest, it probably affects you, too. The reason is that there are more attractive distractions than ever before. We are primed to notice things, but once upon a time, there wasn't so much to notice all at once. This TED-Ed lesson explains how distractibility is normal and natural, and trying to focus in a distracting environment is hard. But it's worth working on for yourself. (via

Laughing Squid)

items.title: Elderly Dog Benefits From Pilates
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Weasel is an almost 16-year-old golden retriever in Hawaii. That's an advanced age, especially for a big dog. His family wanted to do anything they could to help him, and started Weasel on physical therapy. His human Jillian is a pilates instructor, so she started taking him to her studio for gentle workouts. And Weasel showed that his 16 years brought him a lot of smarts even as it was taking his physical strength- he copied her moves! Jillian calls these workouts "paw-lates."

Progress was slow, but it was progress, as the dog gained strength and flexibility. And while his face is still white, he now has the mobility of a much younger dog- most of the time. He still needs a little help every now and then, but don't we all? You can see more of Weasel's fitness journey

items.title: All About Burger King
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: Burger King was born soon after McDonald's as a fast food burger outlet. It was first called Insta-Burger King, and they sold Insta-Burgers. That didn't last all that long, but what stayed was the idea of a flame-broiled burger being better than one that was fried. Still, Burger King tried, but could never overtake McDonald's as the number one burger outlet. They even fell to third for a time when Wendy's peaked. They always had the classic Whopper, but Burger King also became quite famous for their creepy king with a plastic face mascot and for the bizarre promotions they staged, some of which were so bad they disappeared before you ever heard of them. However, in the last few years, Burger King is trying some new ideas, the most intriguing being improvements to the food. Is it working? The comments are split, with half lauding delicious Burger King meals and the other half complaining about them. So... your mileage may vary.

items.title: Why Your Shoes Come Untied
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Why do your shoes laces keep untying themselves? It could be because you're out there running all the time, which vibrates your shoes until the knot loosens. Yeah, that's not the case for most of us. It could be because you're tying them wrong. We are supposed to use a reef knot, a term I'd never heard, essentially a square knot with loops for easy untying. Yet some people tie a granny knot, which doesn't hold well at all. There are other knots that people swear by, but you have to have the motivation to learn them. Kids' shoes come untied all the time because they are so active and inattentive, so I used to double tie my kids' shoes or use those plastic clips to keep the knot in place. 

My feet are small, so I buy shoes from the kids' section because they cost less. My current tennis shoes are tied, then have a velcro strap that closes right over the knot, so no worries. If you need some help keeping your shoes tied, astrophysicist Josie Peters has the science of shoelaces to help you out. (via Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Atlantic Ocean is Acting Weird
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
We've heard of the Gulf Stream, but it's just a part of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC). AMOC flows one way on the surface, and then a different direction in the lower depths of the ocean. This explains why the coldest regions of the continental US are at the same latitudes as the warmest parts of Europe. We will also be introduced to the "cold blob" in the ocean. But this system has shown some changes lately, thanks to glacial melting in Greenland. What does that mean for us?

The effects would be felt in Europe first, but it may affect other parts of the world as well. When will all this happen? Scientists are leery of assigning a date to the point of no return, or the point of environmental collapse. Other factors may be in play, and we can't say that today's trajectory will not change. Still, ocean currents that have been stable for a few thousand years suddenly starting to change can't be a good thing.

items.title: Is It Too Early To Decorate For Christmas?
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
When I was a kid, my parents would pull out the Christmas decorations after Thanksgiving. When I had kids, we'd gradually start decorating when they started asking about it, which was right after Halloween. After they left home, I always made it a point to have the outdoor Christmas lights up to greet my Thanksgiving guests (we usually have the feast at suppertime). I ask my kids to put up the tree and the ornaments when they are here for Thanksgiving. 

I get a kick out of noticing how my neighbors do it. Some just replace Halloween decor with Christmas, either on November first or sometime in December when the skeletons get really dirty. Some even combine the two holidays on their lawn. I don't decorate for Halloween anymore. 

This year, Princess can't come because of her husband's work schedule, and Dr. Dolittle only has one day off, so she and her husband won't have time to help decorate. I guess I better get started on the house prep. I have to move furniture to get the tree up, and I want to mop the floor in between. Hauling heavy stuff from the basement has to be done a little at a time, and during daylight. Outside lights take a couple of days because there are few hours that are warm enough. The logistics get harder every year, but it's still a lot of fun. And it gives me an excuse for not raking leaves until December.

items.title: Hi
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The entire YouTube description for the latest video from Bill Wurtz (previously at Neatorama) is "oops, no ai". What's the story? There is none. This is just following a guy around as he moves through his day, constantly distracted by something else and accomplishing very little along the way. He does get his roof done, but the actual work was done by someone else. 

Is Hi a song? No, but there are musical elements to it here and there. The real genius is in two-second snippets of philosophical thoughts that only make sense when they are taken out of context. The context is a nonsensical framework that seems to be built only to get from one snippet to the next. Or perhaps I am overthinking it. This is probably better enjoyed as the surreal stream of consciousness that it appears to be on the surface. Oh yeah, and there's the Infinity Bus.

items.title: State Borders Are Hard to Draw From Memory
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The online game Borderline challenges us to draw map borders from memory. The United States version has proven to be quite popular. Drawing each state's borders is not easy when you've never done it before, no matter how well you know the US map. Some people are astonishingly good at it. Then you remember that no one is going to try the game unless they think they can do it. 

A compilation map of how all players drew those lines is fascinating. Matt Forrest brings us some insights about that map, specifically that the states with the most complicated borders turn out to be the easiest states to place. The hardest are those with simple, straight borders because they are all together in the American West. (via Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Dying Minutes of World War One
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The Armistice of Compiègne went into effect on November 11, 1918 at 11AM Paris time, to end hostilities in World War One. It effectively ended the war, giving a win to the Allies without Germany having to surrender. Hurried negotiations led to the Armistice order being signed only 6 hours earlier. We mark that point on the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month as the end of the Great War, 108 years ago today. But 11,000 men died on November 11th as the moments ticked down. More were killed afterward, either by soldiers who hadn't received the news of the Armistice, from rare units that refused to quit fighting, or from wounds they received earlier.
Canadian soldier George Lawrence Price, from Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, was serving with the 28th Infantry Battalion on November 11. The 26-year-old was part of a five-man patrol that was checking buildings beside the canal at Ville-sur-Haine, in Mons, for signs of the enemy.

Unfortunately, they found them – a group of German soldiers in the process of setting up machine guns on a wall overlooking the canal. There was an exchange of fire; both sides took cover and the Germans retreated.

The Canadians began to follow, but just as George stepped out onto the street he was shot in the chest by a German sniper. Dragged into a nearby house, he was treated by a local nurse, but there was little she could do.

George Price died soon after, at 10.58am… just two minutes before the armistice.
Read the stories of the last men to die in World War I at historywithatwist. (via Strange Company)

items.title: Five Species That Harness Wildfires
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
For most animals, plants, and other life forms, fire is the worst thing that can happen. It's deadly, and even if you escape, your environment is ruined. But wildfires have always been a part of earth's activities, and some species have evolved to use it to their benefit. For example, the fire lily bulb stays dormant in the ground until after a wildfire rages through. Then it grows and blooms without competition from other plants!  

Plants that grow in the ashes of a wildfire attracts bugs, which attract birds. It's almost as if there's a system to heal and renew the environment after its devastated by fire. There are other species that are attracted to wildfires, and even one that actively spreads a fire. SciScow introduces us to how all this works. This video has a skippable ad from 6:00 to 6:48.
